content: Aldicarb is a carbamate insecticide with the chemical structure 2-methyl-2-(methylthio)propionaldehyde O-methylcarbamoyloxime. It is the active ingredient in the pesticide Temik, which is effective against various pests, including thrips, aphids, spider mites, lygus bugs, fleahoppers, and leafminers. However, its primary use is as a nematicide. In mammals, aldicarb functions as a cholinesterase inhibitor, which means it prevents the breakdown of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. In cases of severe poisoning, death can occur due to respiratory failure. Aldicarb is also highly toxic to birds. Aldicarb is approved by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) for use by professional pesticide applicators on a range of crops, such as cotton and beans. However, it is not approved for household use. A product known as Tres Pasitos, which contains high concentrations of aldicarb, has been illegally imported into the United States from Mexico and other Latin American countries. This product is extremely toxic to both animals and humans and should not be used. In mammals, aldicarb acts as a fast-acting cholinesterase inhibitor, leading to the rapid accumulation of acetylcholine at the synaptic cleft. It is commonly used in research to study cholinergic neurotransmission in simple organisms, such as the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Extremely high doses can be fatal, as they can cause paralysis of the respiratory system.
